title: Interferometric Readout of Momentum-Space Topology in a Programmable Dissipative Photonic Circuit
authors: Andrea Cataldo, Emil J. Bergholtz, Daniel Leykam, Jun Gao, Ali W. Elshaari
abstract: Topology under non-Hermitian dynamics is encoded in the phase of the bulk evolution, yet strong dissipation suppresses the amplitudes carrying it. We resolve this using a programmable photonic integrated circuit that implements such dynamics in synthetic momentum space through unitary dilation, with the phase recovered by phase-shifted interferometry. For the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, the method distinguishes trivial and non-trivial Zak phases and yields a coherence winding $q=\pm 1$ induced by an exceptional point. Extending to a synthetic torus via a Rice-Mele pump gives the first Chern number $\mathrm{Ch}_1=0,1$ for trivial and non-trivial cycles, showing a programmable route to momentum-space topology under strongly dissipative non-Hermitian dynamics.
summary: This paper presents a novel experimental technique using programmable photonic circuits to measure topological invariants in non-Hermitian systems, overcoming the challenge posed by strong dissipation. By implementing the dynamics in synthetic momentum space and using phase-shifted interferometry, the authors successfully read out quantities like the Zak phase and the first Chern number. This establishes a programmable platform for studying momentum-space topology in open quantum systems.
main_problem: The core challenge is reading out topological information encoded in the phase of the bulk evolution in non-Hermitian systems, as this phase is typically suppressed by strong dissipation.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a programmable method using photonic circuits to measure topological invariants, such as the Zak phase and the first Chern number, in the presence of strong dissipation.
method: They employ a programmable photonic integrated circuit to simulate non-Hermitian dynamics, embedding the non-unitary evolution into a unitary one via Sz.-Nagy dilation, and then use phase-shifted interferometry to recover the phase information.
model_or_system: The study uses the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model and extends it to a synthetic torus via a Rice-Mele pump. The dynamics are realized in a programmable photonic integrated circuit (PIC) simulating synthetic momentum space.
key_observables: Zak phase (Zacc), coherence winding (q), and the first Chern number (Ch_1).
important_parameters: Dissipation strength ($\gamma$), coupling constants ($j_1, j_2$), and the parameters defining the pump cycle.
main_assumptions: The method does not require real-space boundaries or spectrally resolved edge modes, though phase readout is ill-conditioned where coherence approaches zero.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SSH lattice and band splitting, the interferometric readout scheme, the extraction of the Zak phase and EP-induced winding, and the extension to a synthetic torus showing the reconstructed coherence and inferred Ch_1.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem (dissipation suppressing phase) to detailing the simulation platform (PIC, unitary dilation), presenting the measurement techniques (interferometry for phase/coherence), and finally demonstrating the measurement of topological invariants (Zak phase, Ch_1) for both 1D and 2D synthetic systems.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it merges concepts from open quantum systems (dissipation, non-Hermiticity) with advanced quantum optics/photonics platforms to measure fundamental topological properties, providing a concrete experimental roadmap for studying non-Hermitian topology.

Fig. 3(a) shows Zacc(k, t) for the non-trivial and trivial cases. In the non-trivial case, it increases progressively with k and reaches nearly π at the boundary, consistent with a net winding. In the trivial case, it shows only a small excursion and returns nearly to zero at the end, indicating vanishing net winding. This behavior is con- sistent with the underlying model, where f(k) encloses the origin in the former case, whereas it does not in the latter. The distinction of topology is thus already evi- dent throughout the accumulated phase trace.
